t.2.17.1: But Rāma, deeply distressed and sighing like an elephant, went, self-controlled, together with his brother to his mother's inner apartments.
t.2.17.2: There he saw an aged man, held in the highest honor, seated at the door of the house, and many others standing there.
t.2.17.3: Having entered the first courtyard, he saw in the second the aged brāhmaṇas, rich in Vedic learning, who had been duly honored by the king.
t.2.17.4: Having bowed to those elders, Rāma saw in the third courtyard women, both old and young, intent on guarding the doors.
t.2.17.6: Then Queen Kausalyā too, having passed the night with a composed mind, at daybreak performed worship of Viṣṇu, desiring the welfare of her son.
t.2.17.5: Having hailed those overjoyed ones and entered the house, the women then hastily announced the welcome news to Rāma's mother.
t.2.17.7: She, clad in linen, joyful and ever devoted to her vows, was then offering oblations into the fire with sacred mantras, having performed the auspicious rites.
t.2.17.8: Then Rāma, having entered his mother's splendid inner apartments, saw his mother there offering oblations into the sacred fire.
t.2.17.9: Seeing her son, the delight of his mother, come to her after a long time, she stepped forward to meet him, overjoyed, as a mare goes to her foal.
t.2.17.10: Out of a mother's tender love for her son, Kausalyā spoke these words, pleasing and beneficial, to Rāghava, her own invincible son.
t.2.17.11: May you attain the long life and the fame of the aged, virtuous, great-souled royal seers, and the dharma established in your family.
t.2.17.12: Behold your father the king, true to his promise, O Rāghava, for this very day that righteous-souled one will consecrate you as heir apparent.
t.2.17.13: Rāghava, stretching forth his joined palms a little, spoke something to his mother; humble by nature and bowed down then out of reverence, he addressed her.
t.2.17.14: O lady, surely you do not know that a great peril has come upon us; this will bring grief to you, to Vaidehī, and to Lakṣmaṇa.
t.2.17.15: For fourteen years I shall dwell in the lonely forest, living like a sage on honey, roots and fruits, having given up meat.
t.2.17.16: The great king is bestowing the office of crown prince upon Bharata, while me he is banishing to the Daṇḍaka forest as an ascetic.
t.2.17.17: Seeing his mother, who was unaccustomed to sorrow, fallen like a plantain tree and bereft of her senses, Rāma raised her up.
t.2.17.18: Like a mare that has been driven hard and has rolled on the ground, she rose up wretched, her whole body smeared with dust, and he stroked her with his hand.
t.2.17.19: She, accustomed to happiness yet now stricken with sorrow, spoke to Rāghava, that tiger among men, who was seated before her, while Lakṣmaṇa listened.
t.2.17.20: O son, O Rāghava, if you had never been born to bring me sorrow, then I, though childless, would not have had to see a grief greater than this.
t.2.17.21: Indeed, a barren woman knows but one human sorrow, the anguish of thinking, 'I am childless'; truly, my son, there is no other.
t.2.17.22: Never before have I known any blessing or happiness through my husband's power; "I may yet see it in my son": this, O Rāma, is the hope I have held.
t.2.17.23: Though I am the highest, I shall have to hear many unpleasant words from my inferior co-wives, who pierce the heart. What could ever be more painful than this for women?
t.2.17.24: Even while you were near, I was spurned like this; how much worse will it be when you have gone away, my son? Surely death alone awaits me.
t.2.17.25: Whoever serves me or even follows my wishes, that person, on seeing Kaikeyī's son, no longer speaks to me.
t.2.17.26: Ten and seven years have passed since you were born, O Rāghava, while I have longed for an end to my sorrow.
t.2.17.27: With fasts, with religious observances, and with many toils, you were reared with hardship and in vain by me, ill-fated woman that I am.
t.2.17.29: Surely for me alone there is no death, nor is there any room for me in the abode of Yama, since Antaka does not wish to carry me off this very day, as a lion forcibly seizes a weeping doe.
t.2.17.28: I think this heart of mine must indeed be hard, since it does not burst apart, as the bank of a great river does in the rainy season when struck by the new waters.
t.2.17.31: This indeed is my sorrow: that my vows, my gifts and my acts of self-restraint have been in vain, and the austerity I practised for the sake of a child has proved utterly fruitless, like seed sown in barren, salty soil.
t.2.17.30: Surely my heart is hard, made of iron, since it does not break nor burst apart upon the ground, though my body is assailed by this grief; truly, death does not come before its appointed time.
t.2.17.32: If anyone worn down by heavy sorrow could gain death untimely by his own wish, then this very day I would have gone to the assembly of the departed, without you, like a cow bereft of her calf.
t.2.17.33: Then, looking at Rāghava and learning of the great calamity, she, unable to bear it, lamented long and bitterly in her deep distress, like a kiṃnarī who sees her son bound.
